A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ToMoE. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated results between v1's Appendices A–E and v2's Appendices A–F.

before.justification: v1 reports original ToMoE perplexity and zero-shot evaluation results, loss and dataset ablations, and expert analyses in the main text and appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds MoE comparisons, additional benchmarks, component ablations, and inference-throughput measurements.

M1.justification: The core architecture, expert construction, routing, and frozen-weight training remain the same. However, Section 3.4 changes the load-balancing probability calculation from explicitly defined softmax in v1 to GSmax in v2 without explaining whether this represents a changed calculation or inconsistent notation. An actual loss modification cannot be established reliably.

E1.justification: v2 adds evaluated BoolQ, SciQ, TruthfulQA, and MMLU benchmarks in Tables 5–6 and Figure 10, substantially broadening task coverage beyond the original language-modeling and five commonsense benchmarks. The original training datasets and evaluation coverage are retained.

E2.justification: Tables 4–6 add evaluated LLaMA-MoE, G-MoEfication, LLaMA-MoE-v2, and CMoE comparators, including multiple configurations and fine-tuned variants. This introduces a substantial direct MoE-construction comparison group. The original structural and semi-structured pruning comparators remain represented.

E3.justification: Alongside the retained zero-shot protocols, v2 introduces 32-shot BoolQ, 5-shot WinoGrande and MMLU, 25-shot ARC-c, and 10-shot HellaSwag evaluations. It also introduces throughput measurements at batch sizes 512, 1024, and 1536. These are additional evaluation designs; the original default 10,000-iteration training setup remains unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained loss, dataset, and expert-count analyses, Table 13 tests local embeddings, head pruning, removal of VO routing, and temperature sensitivity. Figure 4 adds aggregate expert-utilization analysis, Figure 10 examines the MMLU accuracy–parameter trade-off, and Table 15 examines throughput scaling with batch size.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run summaries, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The retained expert-width boxplots describe variation among experts rather than uncertainty across experimental runs.

E6.justification: Original benchmark values are retained, including LLaMA-2 rows relocated from Table 3 to Table 12. v2 adds substantial MoE, MMLU, ablation, and throughput results: Table 13 reports 56.07 for full ToMoE versus 44.99 for head pruning, and Table 15 reports 2360.38–2919.45 tokens/s across batch sizes. Section 4.3 also incorrectly redescribes the unchanged 3.14-point advantage over ModeGPT-Alpaca as '3.14 times'.

T1.justification: New Appendix F derives the effective query–key width from overlapping binary pruning masks, showing that it reaches the allocated width K only when the masks coincide. This adds a focused mathematical justification to the qualitative concern already stated in v1 Appendix A.2.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction broaden the central performance claim from outperforming structural pruning to outperforming both pruning and MoE-construction techniques. Detailed analysis becomes an additional stated contribution. The original claims about uncovering experts without updating pretrained weights and jointly learning routing and expert configurations remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations linking the modest VO-routing benefit to small head dimensions and poor head-pruning performance to distorted attention features. It also discusses temperature robustness, recommends fewer than 16 experts, and qualifies comparable throughput by sufficiently large batch size. Existing interpretations of expert semantics and width allocation are retained.

D1.justification: The abstract adds a code-availability statement and repository address. New comparisons disclose training-token budgets and the matched-iteration fine-tuning setting for LLaMA-MoE. The detailed module configurations, optimizer settings, GPU allocations, and data-processing instructions already present in v1 remain substantially unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 expands positioning against contextual sparsity through Deja Vu, CATS, and structured-sparsity work, and broadens dense-to-MoE discussion and comparisons through MoEfication, generalized MoEfication, LLaMA-MoE-v2, and CMoE. This substantially expands the prior-work context for its unified expert-construction and router-training claim.

P1.justification: v2 rewrites the abstract, condenses the introductory background, edits method explanations and notation, updates author information, and removes the Impact Statement. The main section sequence and much of the existing method and appendix prose remain intact.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from a two-column conference layout to a single-column journal layout with substantially different front matter and table placement. v2 adds comparison and ablation tables and new plots, moves part of Table 3 into appendix Table 12, and combines v1 Figures 5–6 into v2 Figure 6.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses an important gap in v1: a dense-to-MoE method was evaluated mainly against pruning. Direct MoE comparisons, component validation, and measured throughput materially strengthen the evidence for its contribution. These gains outweigh new reporting problems, although the broader superiority claim needs qualification: Table 6 reports 57.40 for ToMoE versus 59.61 and 59.31 for LLaMA-MoE-v2, with very different training-token budgets. Those results support an efficiency–accuracy trade-off.
